question: Which extra interaction law gives consistent dynamics, and when does a single-port induced interaction actually bind?
contracts: Test Hermitian completion of the original electron face0spin0 -> proton AB:x arrow, with arbitrary complex coupling g. It adds an adjoint transfer and acts on a direct sum, not the two-particle sector.

Declare a separate pair-sector quadratic potential -kappa C^dagger C localized at radial site1, kappa>0, where C is the projected normalized-encoder port map. This is a new energy law, not an ordinary transfer arrow already in the source.

Declare a relative-coordinate half-line lattice n>=1, Dirichlet origin, kinetic energy t(2I-S-S^dagger), t>0. This coordinate is neither the spinor norm nor the potential direction sphere. No length or energy unit is calibrated.

Separately test an isotropic extension by averaging the fixed-port quadratic projector over the existing24 binary tetrahedral spin actions. This is an additional interaction permission, not implied by the one arrow. Preserve total interaction trace, so each spin receives half the fixed-port strength.
rivals: A directed transfer is already a closed-system Hamiltonian
Negative finite-sector level splitting establishes particle binding
Spinorial symmetry permits a scalar proton/electron direct-sum mixing
An arbitrarily weak boundary-site attraction necessarily binds on this half-line
falsifier: Exact weighted adjoint and unitarity failures, symmetry obstruction, or failure of the purported bound state boundary/bulk equations, normalizability or threshold proof.
scope: Conditional mathematical dynamics and binding in a newly declared lattice model. No derivation of Coulomb law, mass, charge, physical time, spatial scale or hydrogen binding. Existing potential and spinor carriers remain retained.
